lead: A real oscillator loses energy to friction, so its amplitude falls with time. This is damping. A periodic push can replace that energy, and the response becomes large when the push frequency matches a natural frequency. That is resonance. The same physics explains a car shock absorber settling after a speed breaker, a radio tuning to one station, a bridge swaying in wind, and a piezoelectric crystal vibrating strongly at its thickness resonance.
prereq: You need 2.1 Simple harmonic motion: x = A cos(ω₀t + φ), ω₀ = √(k/m), and energy in an oscillator.

blocks.text: Damping is the loss of oscillator energy to friction or other resistance. For slow motion in air or oil, take a damping force F_b = −b v, where v is speed in m/s and b is the damping constant in kg/s. Newton's second law for mass m in kg on a spring of stiffness k in N/m gives m x'' + b x' + k x = 0. The natural angular frequency is ω₀ = √(k/m) in rad/s. The damping ratio ζ = b/(2√(mk)) is dimensionless and compares damping with the critical value.
x = A e^(−bt/(2m)) cos(ω_d t + φ),  ω_d = √(ω₀² − (b/2m)²)
blocks.where: x is displacement in m; A is the amplitude coefficient at t = 0 in m, and the actual starting displacement is x(0) = A cos φ; b is damping constant in kg/s; m is mass in kg; φ is initial phase in rad; ω_d is damped angular frequency in rad/s; ω₀ = √(k/m) is natural angular frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: For ζ < 1 the oscillator is underdamped: the motion oscillates with steadily falling amplitude at frequency ω_d. The factor e^(−bt/(2m)) is the decaying envelope. The damped period is T_d = 2π/ω_d. The logarithmic decrement is δ = (b/2m)T_d = 2πζ/√(1−ζ²), the log ratio of successive peak amplitudes. Because ω_d < ω₀, damping lowers the observed frequency; do not call ω_d the natural frequency. For ζ = 1 (critical damping) the motion returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; critical damping occurs at b = 2√(mk). For ζ > 1 (overdamping) it returns more slowly, also without oscillation. A car shock absorber is designed near critical so the body settles after a speed breaker without bouncing.

A forced oscillator is driven by an external periodic force. The equation is m x'' + b x' + k x = F₀ cos ωt, where F₀ is the force amplitude in N and ω is the drive angular frequency in rad/s. The drive supplies energy every cycle; damping removes it. After start-up transients die out, the steady motion is x = A cos(ωt − φ).

blocks.where: A is steady amplitude in m; F₀ is driving force amplitude in N; m is mass in kg; ω is drive angular frequency in rad/s; ω₀ = √(k/m) is natural angular frequency in rad/s; b is damping constant in kg/s.

blocks.text: At very low ω, A ≈ F₀/k: the spring controls and the mass follows the force. At very high ω, A → 0: the mass cannot keep up. Near ω = ω₀ the first term in the denominator is small. If b is small, A becomes large. This is resonance. The phase lag φ satisfies tan φ = (bω/m)/(ω₀² − ω²). It is small below resonance, passes 90° at ω = ω₀, and approaches 180° above resonance. The displacement amplitude peaks at ω_r = √(ω₀² − b²/(2m²)) when b² < 2mk. This amplitude resonance lies slightly below ω₀; only for zero damping is it exactly at ω₀. Some syllabi call this driven oscillation.

The quality factor Q measures how sharp a resonance is. Q = ω₀/Δω, where Δω is the full width of the power resonance curve at half its maximum value, in rad/s. The two frequencies at half power are ω₁ and ω₂, so Δω = ω₂ − ω₁. For the damped oscillator Q = mω₀/b = 1/(2ζ). High Q means small damping: a tall narrow peak, a long ringing time, and many cycles to build up or decay. Low Q means heavy damping: a low broad peak and quick settling. At ω = ω₀, for light damping, A ≈ F₀/(bω₀). A radio receiver uses a high-Q circuit to pick one station and reject nearby ones. A machine support uses damping to keep Q low and avoid large vibration. The figure shows two response curves with the same natural frequency; the lightly damped one has the taller, narrower peak near ω/ω₀ = 1.

figure.caption: Amplitude response of a driven damped oscillator. The lightly damped curve is tall and narrow near ω/ω₀ = 1; the moderately damped curve is lower and broader.

spec.aria: Two resonance curves: the lightly damped curve has a tall narrow peak near ω/ω₀ = 1, the moderately damped curve a low broad one.

examples.question: A 0.20 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 80 N/m has damping constant b = 0.40 kg/s. Find the natural angular frequency ω₀, the damping ratio ζ, and the damped angular frequency ω_d.
steps: Write the data: m = 0.20 kg, k = 80 N/m, b = 0.40 kg/s.
Damping ratio: ζ = b/(2√(mk)) = 0.40/(2√(0.20 × 80)) = 0.40/(2 × 4) = 0.05. Since ζ < 1, the motion is underdamped.
examples.answer: ω₀ = 20 rad/s, ζ = 0.05, and ω_d ≈ 19.97 rad/s.
examples.check:
import math
m = 0.20
k = 80.0
b = 0.40
omega0 = math.sqrt(k/m)
zeta = b/(2*math.sqrt(m*k))
omega_d = math.sqrt(omega0**2 - (b/(2*m))**2)
print(round(omega0, 2))
print(round(zeta, 2))
print(round(omega_d, 2))

traps: Using ω_d as the natural frequency. ω_d = √(ω₀² − (b/2m)²) is the damped frequency; ω₀ = √(k/m) is the natural frequency.
Saying resonance is always exactly at ω₀. Amplitude resonance is at ω_r = √(ω₀² − b²/(2m²)); phase lag is 90° at ω₀.
Mixing ζ with b. ζ = b/(2√(mk)) is dimensionless; b has units kg/s.
Dropping the factor 2 in b/(2m). The amplitude envelope is e^(−bt/(2m)), not e^(−bt/m).
Using the peak amplitude formula at arbitrary ω. A(ω) must be computed from the full denominator.

quiz.q: Define damping ratio ζ and give its formula for mass m, stiffness k and damping constant b.
quiz.a: ζ = b/(2√(mk)); it is dimensionless and compares damping with critical damping.

quiz.q: Why is the underdamped frequency ω_d lower than ω₀?
quiz.a: Damping adds a resistive term that opposes motion; the solution gives ω_d = √(ω₀² − (b/2m)²), so the square-root term is smaller than ω₀. At ζ = 0 they are equal.

quiz.q: A 0.50 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 50 N/m has b = 0.20 kg/s. Find ζ and ω_d.
A forced oscillator has m = 1 kg, k = 100 N/m, b = 2 kg/s, F₀ = 10 N and drive frequency ω = 10 rad/s. Find the steady amplitude A(ω).
Explain why a bridge can be damaged by soldiers marching in step even if each step is small.
quiz.a: If step frequency is near a natural frequency, each push adds energy in phase; damping may be small, so amplitude builds over many cycles. Large stress can exceed design limits. Breaking step avoids sustained resonance.

quiz.q: Define quality factor Q and give its relation to ζ for the damped oscillator.
quiz.a: Q = ω₀/Δω, where Δω is half-power bandwidth; also Q = mω₀/b = 1/(2ζ).

quiz.q: Why does phase lag pass 90° at ω₀ rather than at amplitude resonance ω_r?
quiz.a: Phase depends on the ratio of damping term to stiffness-minus-inertia term. At ω = ω₀ the stiffness and inertia terms cancel, leaving only damping, so φ = 90°. Amplitude peak is shifted below ω₀ by damping; the two frequencies differ slightly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Damping and resonance design appears in MEMS accelerometers, atomic force microscope cantilevers, seismic tuned mass dampers in tall buildings, and laser cavities. Engineers choose Q and bandwidth together: a high-Q sensor is sensitive but slow, a low-Q sensor is fast but less selective. Search next for quality factor, half-power bandwidth, logarithmic decrement, and tuned mass damper.
